questions.question: A bar of chocolate is cut into 4 equal pieces. You eat 1 piece. What fraction of the whole bar is your piece?
questions.explain: The bar has 4 equal pieces and you have 1, so your piece is 1/4. The total number of equal parts (4) always goes on the bottom.

questions.question: Two friends split one banana into 2 equal halves. Each friend gets 1 half. What fraction of the banana does each friend get?
questions.explain: The banana has 2 equal halves and each friend has 1, so the fraction is 1/2. Put the total parts (2) on the bottom, not on top.

questions.question: A cookie is broken into 3 equal pieces. You give 1 piece to your little sister. What fraction of the whole cookie did she get?
questions.explain: There are 3 equal pieces and your sister has 1, so her piece is 1/3. The number of equal parts (3) always goes on the bottom.

questions.question: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. You take 1 slice for lunch. What fraction of the whole pizza is your slice?
questions.explain: The pizza has 6 equal slices and you have 1, so it is 1/6. More slices means a smaller piece, so 1/6 is smaller than 1/3.

questions.question: At snack time, the teacher cuts a big chocolate bar into 5 equal pieces. Each of 5 students gets 1 piece. What fraction of the bar is each student's piece?
questions.explain: The bar has 5 equal pieces and each student has 1, so the fraction is 1/5. The 5 equal parts go on the bottom.

questions.question: Sam cuts a sandwich into 3 pieces, but one piece is much bigger than the other two. Sam says, 'Each piece is 1/3 of the sandwich.' Is Sam right?
options: No, the pieces must be equal
questions.explain: For a fraction to work, every piece must be the same size. If the pieces are not equal, you cannot call each one 1/3.

questions.question: A watermelon is cut into equal slices. One slice is 1/6 of the whole watermelon. How many equal slices is the watermelon cut into?
questions.explain: The bottom number in 1/6 tells you the total equal parts, so the watermelon has 6 equal slices. The top number (1) is just how many slices you are looking at.

questions.question: A cake is cut into equal pieces. Each piece is 1/4 of the whole cake. A child takes 1 piece for her plate. How many equal pieces was the whole cake cut into?
questions.explain: In 1/4, the bottom number 4 means there are 4 equal pieces in the whole cake. It does not matter that the child only took 1 piece.

questions.question: Mia cuts her banana bread into equal pieces for her family. Each person takes 1 piece. What fraction of the whole bread is one piece?
questions.explain: There are 6 equal pieces, so one piece is 1/6 of the bread. The bottom number counts every piece, not just the ones left over.

questions.question: Two pans of cornbread are the same size. Pan A is shared fairly by 2 kids. Pan B is shared fairly by 4 kids. Who gets a bigger piece?
questions.explain: Pan A is cut into 2 equal parts, so each kid there gets 1/2, and 1/2 is bigger than 1/4. Sharing with more kids makes each piece smaller.

questions.question: Leo has one pita bread. He wants to share it fairly with his 3 friends, so all 4 get the same amount. What should Leo do?
questions.explain: Four kids share, so the pita needs 4 equal parts and each part is 1/4. Leo must count himself, and every part must be the same size.

questions.question: Ella pours one full bottle of apple juice into 4 cups. She puts the same amount in every cup. What fraction of the bottle is in one cup?
questions.explain: The bottle fills 4 equal cups, so one cup holds 1/4 of the bottle. The bottom number counts all the equal shares, not just the other ones.

questions.question: Noah shares his fruit bar fairly with 2 friends. Then 3 more friends come, so he shares the same bar fairly with all 6 kids. When was each share bigger?
questions.explain: Three kids get 1/3 each, but six kids get only 1/6 each. More sharers means each share is smaller, not bigger.

questions.question: Sofia cuts her flatbread into 3 equal strips. Then she cuts each strip into 2 equal pieces. Each friend takes 1 of these pieces. What fraction of the flatbread is one piece?
questions.explain: Cutting the 3 strips in half makes 6 equal pieces, so one piece is 1/6. Do not stop at 3 strips, count the pieces after the second cut.

questions.question: Ruby cuts her carrot loaf into 5 equal pieces and takes 1 piece. She says her piece is 1/4 of the loaf, because 4 pieces are left. What should Ruby say?
questions.explain: The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole loaf has, and that is 5, so her piece is 1/5. The 4 pieces left are not the whole loaf.

questions.question: One pumpkin pie is shared fairly at a family dinner. Each person takes 1 piece, and each piece is 1/7 of the pie. Two of the people are grown-ups. How many children are at the dinner?
questions.explain: Each piece is 1/7, so the pie was cut into 7 equal pieces for 7 people. Then take away the 2 grown-ups: 7 - 2 = 5 children.
